chunks: Abu Nasr Hibatullah ibn Muhammad said: Abu al-Hasan ibn Kibriya al-Nuubakhti narrated to us that: It reached Shaykh Abu al-Qasim (may Allah be pleased with him) that a doorman of his, stationed at the first door, had cursed Muawiyah and insulted him, so he ordered his dismissal and removal from his service. He remained for a long period asking about his matter, and by Allah, he did not return him to his service, and some of the family took him and employed him with them. All of this was due to dissimulation (Taqiyyah).

key_terms.التَّقِيَّة: Dissimulation; concealing one's true beliefs or actions to avoid harm in times of political or religious pressure.
key_terms.الشَّيْخ: The Shaykh; referring to Abu al-Qasim al-Husayni ibn Ruh al-Nawbakhti, a prominent Imamite scholar and contemporary of the Four Imams.
key_terms.مُعَاوِيَة: Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, the Umayyad caliph, often cited in Shia sources as a key figure of the opposing political lineage.

ai.seo_question: Why did Shaykh Abu al-Qasim keep his dismissed doorman waiting for a long time?
ai.summary: This narrative from *Kitab al-Ghayba* illustrates the practical application of *Taqiyyah* by Imam al-Husayn ibn Ruh, the fourth Deputy of the Hidden Imam, who dismissed his doorman for cursing Muawiyah but retained him in a state of suspended service to avoid political repercussions. The delay in full reinstatement highlights the nuanced political strategy employed during the Minor Occultation, where subtle actions were taken to maintain authority while navigating the pressures of the Abbasid caliphate. This incident underscores the scholarly view that *Taqiyyah* was not merely concealment of belief but a dynamic administrative tool for the Deputies.
